---
title: "Lockfile for {baler}"
---

`baler.lock` is a lockfile (like `Cargo.lock` or `poetry.lock` from Python) that pins the exact R package versions (and repos) that `{baler}` resolved the last time you ran `baler lock`. Commit it next to `baler.toml` so later installs, either by you or by anyone else, will reuse those pins instead of re-resolving against CRAN.

Three kinds of R packages are locked: runtime packages under `[dependencies]`, build-time packages under `[compiled-code]`'s `build_deps`, and packages under `[extras]`. Each entry records which of these it is needed for (see `groups` below). On the other hand, `{box}` module dependencies (`[dependencies.baler]`) have no automatic resolve-and-install path as of now, so there is nothing concrete to pin for them. External tools under `[extras.external]` are never locked either, since `{baler}` only checks for them.

## Format

The file is TOML. Format version is currently `2`. Locks written with format version `1` are still read as they are, since a package without `groups` means the same thing in both. The table below summarizes the blocks and fields under `baler.lock`:

| Field | Meaning |
|--------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| `version` | Lock *format* version (not a package version). Defaults to the current format version if omitted when reading. |
| `r_version` | The R version that produced this lock, e.g. `"4.2.0"`. This is totally optional, and it has rather no use. This is only written when `baler lock` is run with `--with-rver`. The constraint actually enforced lives in `baler.toml`'s `r_version` field, checked separately at lock and install time (see below). |
| `[[package]]` | One entry per pinned R package. Entries are written sorted by `name` so the file stays stable and diffable. |
| `name` | Package name as it appears on the repo. |
| `version` | Exact semver string baler resolved (e.g. `"1.2.2"`). |
| `repo` | Repo URL used for that resolution (default CRAN mirror, or an explicit repo from `[dependencies]`). |
| `groups` | What the package is needed for: `runtime`, `build` (from `[compiled-code]`), or `extras` (from `[extras]`). When omitted, the package is needed at runtime only, which is the common case. A package needed by more than one group lists all of them, `runtime` included. An unknown group name is a parse error, so a typo fails loudly. |

Here's an example:

``` toml
version = 2

[[package]]
name = "Rcpp"
version = "1.0.12"
repo = "https://cloud.r-project.org"
groups = ["runtime", "build"]

[[package]]
name = "dplyr"
version = "1.1.3"
repo = "https://cloud.r-project.org"

[[package]]
name = "rlang"
version = "1.2.0"
repo = "https://cloud.r-project.org"

[[package]]
name = "testthat"
version = "3.2.1"
repo = "https://cloud.r-project.org"
groups = ["extras"]
```

Groups are worked out per dependency set, not only for the packages you declare yourself. A package that is only pulled in by `testthat` is `extras` too, and a package that both a runtime dependency and a build dependency need is tagged with both.

`r_version` isn't in the example above since it's not written by default. This field is totally optional and only generated when you pass `--with-rver` to `baler lock` (see below). Here's what it looks like when you do:

``` toml
version = 2
r_version = "4.2.0"

[[package]]
name = "dplyr"
version = "1.1.3"
repo = "https://cloud.r-project.org"
```

## Writing the lock

Generating the lockfile runs a simple command through `baler lock <path/of/the/proj>`, just isn't the same process as `Cargo.lock` being generated through builds. Run the following command and this will generate the certain lockfile that pins the dependencies:

``` bash
baler lock .
```

What happens is that `{baler}` will read and validate `baler.toml` (the same checks `baler install` makes: a strict semver `version`, consistent keys in each `[dependencies.baler]` entry, and bare command names under `[extras.external]`), then resolves the runtime packages, the `[compiled-code]` build deps, and the `[extras]` packages, each on its own (honoring any existing lock unless you pass `--update`). The three sets are merged into one entry per package, and `baler.lock` is written next to `baler.toml`. If the sets resolve the same package to different versions, `baler lock` stops with an error instead of picking one. Align the version constraints in `baler.toml` and run it again. You are also allowed to re-resolve the pinned dependencies under the lockfile by passing `--update`. Here's an example:

``` bash
baler lock . --update
```

`--update` discards the existing lock and re-resolves everything from scratch. Use it when you intentionally want newer upstream versions. A project with no dependencies resolves to an empty set: the lock is still there written, but with no `[[package]]` entries.

### Recording the R version

By default, the lock doesn't record which R wrote it. Let's say two people on different R versions running `baler lock` against the same `baler.toml` should get the exact same `[[package]]` output, and if `r_version` was always written that'd turn into a pointless diff every time. Pass `--with-rver` if you want it recorded anyway:

``` bash
baler lock . --with-rver
```

It is added as part of proposal, and this can be mostly useful for debugging. Say someone reports a weird install and you want to know what R wrote their lock. It still doesn't change or dictate what's enforced at install, that's still `baler.toml`'s `r_version` job.

### Removing the lock

You can manually delete `baler.lock` whatever, whenever, and however you want. `{baler}` just adds another option on `baler lock` command through passing `--remove`, which deletes `baler.lock` and stops there. Nothing will be resolved on `{baler}` once `baler.lock`, but nothing is broken, so rest assured. Also, `--update` / `--with-rver` are ignored if you pass them alongside `--remove`. There's a nuance and that is to *safely remove the lockfile*. To repeat, a missing lock just means `{baler}` resolves `[dependencies]` under `baler.toml` fresh, same as a project that never had one.

``` bash
baler lock . --remove
```

## How installs use the lock

Almost nothing throws a failure when the module doesn't have a lockfile. When we say "almost", `{baler}` still conveniently resolves the usual way to install the package dependencies, although having a lockfile is nice-to-have for better reproducibility. The problem is that when you DO have a lockfile but malformed and/or unreadable will throw a failure. That's why a broken lock file fails loudly instead of being silently ignored.

When `baler.lock` is present in the project root:

-   Every runtime package listed in the lock, including the transitive ones you never declared, is installed at that [exact version]{.underline} and repo.
-   Packages tagged only `build` or `extras` stay pinned in the lock, but a normal install does not install them. Build packages are installed when the module's native code is built, and `[extras]` packages are not installed by `baler install` yet.
-   A package declared in `baler.toml` but missing from the lock, or one whose `repo` changed, is an error telling you the lock is stale. Run `baler lock --update` and commit the new lock.

## R version

`{baler}` still cares about the R version, just not through the lock. `baler.toml`'s `[project]` `r_version` is a version constraint, like `">=4.4.0"` or `"^4.4.0"`, written the same way you'd write a `[dependencies]` version. Both `baler lock` and `baler install` check the R on `PATH` against this constraint before doing anything else, and if it doesn't match, that's a hard error, not a warning.

`baler.lock`'s `r_version` field is different. It just records what R wrote the lock, rather than some constraints, and only if you passed `--with-rver`. What's actually enforced is always `baler.toml`'s floor, checked against whatever R you have right now. What you need to do is to write it as a floor like `">=4.4.0"`, not an exact pin. An exact pin means only people on that one exact R version can even install the module.

## Design notes

1.  Packages are sorted by name on write so routine re-locks do not produce noisy diffs when the resolved graph is unchanged.
2.  An invalid version string inside a lock entry fails hard on lookup rather than falling through to a fresh resolve.
3.  The lock format version field exists so future schema changes can be detected and handled without silently misreading old locks. Version `2` only added the optional `groups` field.
4.  `r_version` is opt-in (`--with-rver`) rather than always written, for the same diff-stability reason as (1): it depends on the machine running `baler lock`, not on `baler.toml`, so recording it unconditionally would defeat (1) for any two contributors on different R installs.
5.  `groups` is omitted for runtime-only packages, so a project with no `[compiled-code]` build deps and no `[extras]` writes the same entries as before.
6.  Versions of external tools are never written to the lock. They depend on the machine, not on `baler.toml`, which is the same reasoning as (4).
